title: Rulers Who Devour, Prophets for Hire, and Zion Plowed
summary: Micah confronts the rulers of Jacob, who should know justice but tear the flesh from the people as if cooking meat. He condemns prophets who announce peace to those who feed them and war to those who don't, and he declares that God will leave them in darkness without a vision. Filled with the Spirit of the LORD, Micah names the sin of leaders, priests, and prophets who work for money while claiming the LORD is among them, and he announces that Zion will be plowed like a field.
story: This chapter opens the second of Micah's three cycles and contains his most direct attack on Jerusalem's leadership. Chapter 2 exposed the land-grabbers and the preachers who told Micah to be quiet; chapter 3 goes to the top, to the rulers, judges, priests, and prophets who were responsible for justice and truth. It ends with the book's most shocking sentence: Jerusalem and its temple will be reduced to a plowed field and a wooded hill. Immediately after this, chapter 4 opens with the opposite picture, the temple mountain raised above all others. The contrast between 3:12 and 4:1 is one of the sharpest turns in the prophets.
historical:
The chapter reflects Jerusalem in the late eighth century BC, during the reigns of Ahaz and Hezekiah. The city was growing rapidly, in part from refugees fleeing the Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom, and major building projects were under way; archaeologists have found evidence of Jerusalem's expansion onto the western hill in this period, and Hezekiah's tunnel and fortifications belong to it. Micah's charge that leaders "build Zion with bloodshed" (verse 10) may refer to projects built with forced labor or on property seized from the poor.

This chapter has a remarkable afterlife. About a century later, when Jeremiah was on trial for his life for predicting the temple's destruction, some elders defended him by quoting Micah 3:12 word for word and recalling that Hezekiah did not put Micah to death but feared the LORD and sought his favor, so that God relented (Jeremiah 26:17-19). Jerusalem was spared in 701 BC. The prophecy was not canceled, however; the city and temple fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC, and the temple mount was desolate.
cultural:
In Israel, rulers and elders were responsible for judging cases at the city gate and in the royal courts; the law demanded impartial judgment and forbade taking bribes (Exodus 23:8, Deuteronomy 16:19). Priests were to teach the law freely, and prophets to speak God's word regardless of reward. Micah charges all three offices with selling their service: leaders "judge for a bribe", priests "teach for a price", and prophets "practice divination for money" (verse 11).

Prophets were often supported by gifts from those who consulted them (1 Samuel 9:7-8), which created an obvious temptation to tell paying clients what they wanted to hear. Micah describes prophets who "proclaim peace while they chew with their teeth" (verse 5): as long as they are fed, the message is peace (shalom). Divination (verses 6, 7, and 11) refers to techniques for discovering the future, such as reading omens, that the law forbade (Deuteronomy 18:10-14); by linking the prophets with diviners, Micah treats them as no better than pagan fortune tellers. Covering the mouth (verse 7) was a sign of shame or mourning (Leviticus 13:45).
literary: The chapter contains three oracles, each with an accusation and a judgment. Verses 1 to 4 address the rulers, whose treatment of the people is described in the grotesque image of butchering and cooking meat; the judgment is that God will not answer when they cry out. Verses 5 to 8 address the prophets; the judgment is darkness and silence, and Micah contrasts himself with them in verse 8, one of the strongest statements of prophetic calling in the Bible. Verses 9 to 12 address all the leaders together, quote their false confidence ("Is not the LORD among us?"), and end with the verdict on Zion. The repeated call "hear" (verses 1 and 9) marks the divisions, and the word justice (mishpat) appears in verses 1, 8, and 9, framing the chapter around what the leaders should have known.

outline.t: Rulers who devour the people like meat
Prophets who preach for food will get no vision
Micah filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD
Leaders, priests, and prophets for sale

doctrines.note: Leaders who refuse to hear the cries of the oppressed will find that God does not hear their cries (verse 4). The judgment on Zion shows that even God's chosen city and temple are not exempt when its leaders turn it into a machine for injustice.

Micah says he is "filled with power by the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and courage" (verse 8). The Spirit's work here is not ecstatic experience but the moral strength to tell the truth to the powerful.
True prophecy is not for sale. The prophets who shaped their message to their income will be left without vision, while Micah's message comes from God regardless of reward.

words.note: Mishpat, justice. It includes judicial fairness, right order in society, and the protection of the weak. "Should you not know justice?" (verse 1). The word appears three times in the chapter; the leaders should know it, Micah is filled with it, and they despise it.

Shochad, bribe. A gift given to influence a judge. The law warned that a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and twists the words of the righteous (Exodus 23:8). In verse 11 it stands for the corruption of the whole justice system.

Qasam, to divine. Seeking hidden knowledge by omens and techniques, forbidden in Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10). Micah uses it for Jerusalem's prophets, accusing them of turning prophecy into a trade no different from pagan fortune telling.

Ruach, spirit. In verse 8 it is the Spirit of the LORD who fills Micah with power, justice, and courage. The contrast with 2:11, where the false preacher is a "man of wind" (the same word), is deliberate: Micah has the Spirit, they have only wind.

christ: Micah's attack on religious leaders who serve for money and on a temple that has become a symbol of false security is echoed in the ministry of Jesus. Jesus drove the money-changers from the temple, calling it a house of prayer that had been made a den of robbers (Mark 11:15-17), and he foretold the temple's destruction (Mark 13:1-2), which happened in AD 70. He condemned religious leaders who devoured widows' houses (Mark 12:40). Like Micah, Jesus ministered in the power of the Spirit to proclaim good news to the poor (Luke 4:18). The link is thematic: Jesus stands in the line of prophets like Micah, and he is also the one in whom God's true temple is found (John 2:19-21).

hard.q: If Micah said Zion would be plowed like a field and it did not happen in his lifetime, was he wrong?
hard.a: Jeremiah 26:17-19 gives the Bible's own answer. The elders recalled that Hezekiah responded to Micah's warning with repentance, and the LORD relented from the disaster he had pronounced. On this reading Micah's prophecy was a real warning that achieved its purpose, as Jonah's did in Nineveh. The judgment was delayed, not canceled; Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC when later generations returned to the same sins. Some interpreters add that prophecies of judgment often have a conditional element even when it is not stated (Jeremiah 18:7-10). The episode shows that biblical prophecy is not fortune telling but a word meant to change the hearers.

questions: Micah says the leaders "hate good and love evil". What forms does that take in places of power today, including in churches?
The false prophets preached peace to those who paid them. How might your own words be shaped by who is paying, feeding, or approving of you?
The leaders said, "Is not the LORD among us?" while doing injustice. Where might you be using God's presence as a guarantee instead of a call?
